_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla, typed out on the slip. Each lesson has two: "start" comes on as the lesson opens, and "check" is a short quiz once the lesson's check is done. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies" (none means a plain "Roger. Over."). A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla. This week’s question comes up every time the sky goes grey: will it actually rain, or is it just sulking? Most grey skies never drop a thing, and one kind nearly always does.

replies.say: Grey clouds mean rain, don’t they?
replies.back: Not as often as you’d think. That’s the lesson.

turns.them: Why some days the air bubbles up and some days it lies flat, the lid that spreads heaps into a grey sheet, and the one grey sky that soaks you. Questions at the end, as usual.
Harrow, Walla Walla. Questions. On a hot afternoon the air around gets colder by 12 degrees a kilometre as you go up. A thermal off a stubble field cools at 10. Does it keep rising?

replies.say: Yes. It stays warmer than the air around it.
replies.back: Right. It cools slower than its neighbours, so it keeps its lead. That’s an unstable day.

replies.say: No. It’s cooling, so it sinks.
replies.back: Everything that rises cools. What matters is whether it cools faster or slower than the air around it. Ten is slower than twelve, so it keeps going.

replies.say: Only if it makes a cloud.
replies.back: No cloud needed. Ten is slower than twelve, so it stays warmer than its neighbours and climbs all on its own.

turns.them: A dark grey sheet overhead. Does dark mean rain?

replies.say: Not by itself. Depth matters more.
replies.back: Exactly. A thin sheet can look dark and give nothing but drizzle. It takes a deep cloud to grow drops heavy enough to fall.
A thin sheet can look dark and never give more than drizzle. Depth makes rain, not darkness.
The clock has nothing to do with it. Depth makes rain, not darkness.

turns.them: A lumpy grey sheet with slits of blue has sat overhead all day under high pressure. What is it, and what will it do?

replies.back: Right. Heaps spread under a lid. Grey, but shallow.
Nimbostratus is featureless and hides the sun entirely. Lumps with blue between are stratocumulus, and mostly dry.
Under high pressure, with a lid on? No. That’s stratocumulus, spread flat and mostly dry.

turns.them: Good. Next lesson we climb higher and sort the whole sky.
